common_name: Stayman Apple (Stayman Winesap, Rich Wine-Flavored Keeper Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Stayman produces little viable pollen and needs a separate pollinator variety such as Golden Delicious or Jonathan.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Discovered in Kansas in 1866 by Dr. J. Stayman as a seedling of the older Winesap apple, this cultivar keeps the tangy, wine-like flavor of its parent in a larger, more productive fruit. The dark red skin covers dense, juicy flesh that holds up well in storage and in cooking, and the tree has long been a Mid-Atlantic and Southern favorite for cider and pie making. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the background color turns from green to yellow-green.

common_name: Ginger Gold Apple (First-of-the-Season Crisp Yellow-Green Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ginger Gold ripens in mid-to-late summer, well ahead of most other apples, so pick promptly since fruit can go soft quickly on the tree in warm weather.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Fuji. Found as a chance seedling near a Golden Delicious orchard in Nelson County, Virginia after Hurricane Camille in 1969, the tree was named for the discoverer's wife, Ginger Harvey. It is prized as one of the very first apples ready to harvest each year, well before Gala, with crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh that resists browning after slicing. The pale yellow-green skin sometimes develops a light pink blush in full sun. Because the fruit softens quickly once ripe, it is best picked promptly and used within a few weeks rather than stored long term.

common_name: Akane Apple (Tokyo Rose, Early Scab-Resistant Tart-Sweet Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Akane blooms and ripens early in the season and needs a pollinator such as Jonathan or Golden Delicious that flowers at the same time.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible early-blooming pollinator. Bred in Japan from a cross of Jonathan and Worcester Pearmain and released in 1970, Akane produces small-to-medium, bright red apples with crisp, juicy, tart-sweet flesh reminiscent of Jonathan but with better resistance to apple scab. It ripens in late summer, ahead of most main-season apples, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early harvest without spraying heavily for disease. Fruit is best used fresh or in sauce shortly after picking, as it does not store as long as later-season varieties.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

common_name: Parson Brown Orange (Oldest Commercial Florida Sweet Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Parson Brown is a self-fruitful, early-ripening sweet orange first found growing near Webster, Florida around 1856 and named for the Reverend N.L. Brown who propagated it. It became the first Florida orange of the season to reach market each fall, historically important for growers wanting fruit before Hamlin or Valencia came in. The medium-large fruit has a moderate number of seeds and a mild, sweet flavor that is less intensely sweet than modern seedless oranges but appreciated for its historical role and reliable early cropping. Its relative cold-hardiness among sweet oranges made it a mainstay of the northern Florida citrus belt before hardier hybrids became available.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parson Brown is the earliest-ripening common sweet orange, ready from October, and is notably more cold-tolerant than later-season Florida oranges, which historically made it valuable for the northern edge of the citrus belt.

common_name: Ambersweet Orange (Cold-Hardy Early Hybrid Sweet Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1989 after breeding work in Orlando, Florida, Ambersweet is a complex hybrid combining Clementine mandarin, Orlando tangelo, and sweet orange parentage, developed specifically to withstand occasional hard freezes better than standard sweet oranges while still tasting like a true orange. Fruit ripens unusually early for a sweet orange, often ready by October, with a deep orange rind, easy peeling for an orange type, and rich, low-acid sweetness. The tree's improved cold tolerance has made it a useful option for growers along the cooler margins of the citrus-growing Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun; Ambersweet tolerates more cold than most sweet oranges and ripens very early, from October, extending the citrus season in areas at the cooler edge of the Gulf Coast citrus belt.
